'''Stuart Schreiber''' (born February 6, 1956) is an American chemist who is the Morris Loeb Research Professor at Harvard University,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart L. Schreiber |url=https://chemistry.harvard.edu/people/stuart-l-schreiber |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=chemistry.harvard.edu |language=en}}</ref> a co-founder of the Broad Institute,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-11-23 |title=Stuart L. Schreiber |url=https://www.broadinstitute.org/bios/stuart-l-schreiber |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=Broad Institute |language=en}}</ref> Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator, Emeritus,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart L. Schreiber, PhD {{!}} Investigator Emeriti Profile {{!}} 1994-2018 {{!}} HHMI |url=https://www.hhmi.org/scientists/stuart-l-schreiber |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=www.hhmi.org |language=en}}</ref> and a member of the National Academy of Sciences<ref>{{Cite web |title=Stuart L. Schreiber |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/stuart-l-schreiber-oczblf/ |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=www.nasonline.org}}</ref> and National Academy of Medicine.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The National Academy of Medicine honors Stuart Schreiber |url=https://chemistry.harvard.edu/news/national-academy-medicine-honors-stuart-schreiber |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=chemistry.harvard.edu |date=16 October 2018 |language=en}}</ref> From 2024 to 2025 he led [[Arena BioWorks]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Braner |first=Sarah |date=2025-01-21 |title=Billionaire-backed Arena BioWorks closes less than 2 years after launch |url=https://cen.acs.org/pharmaceuticals/drug-discovery/Billionaire-backed-Arena-BioWorks-closes/103/web/2025/11 |access-date=2025-12-03 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en}}</ref>

His work integrates chemical biology and human biology to advance the science of therapeutics. Key advances include the discovery that small molecules can function as “molecular glues” that promote protein–protein interactions, the co-discovery of mTOR and its role in nutrient-response signaling, the discovery of histone deacetylases and (with Michael Grunstein and David Allis) the demonstration that chromatin marks regulate gene expression, the development and application of diversity-oriented synthesis to microbial therapeutics, and the discovery of vulnerabilities of cancer cells linked to genetic, lineage and cell-state features, including ferroptotic vulnerabilities. His awards include the Wolf Prize in Chemistry and the Arthur Cope Award. His approach to discovering new therapeutics guided many biotechnology companies that he founded, including Vertex Pharmaceuticals and Ariad Pharmaceuticals. He has founded or co-founded 14 biotechnology companies, which have developed 16 first-in-human approved drugs or advanced clinical candidates.

== Early life ==
Schreiber was born on February 6, 1956, in [[Eatontown, New Jersey]], to Mary Geraldine Schreiber and Thomas Sewell Schreiber. From the ages of one to four he lived with his family in Villennes-sur-Seine, a small village in France, where his father was a battalion commander at [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Find an object {{!}} Imperial War Museums |url=https://www.iwm.org.uk/collections/search?query=thomas+s.+schreiber&pageSize=30&media-records=all-records&style=list |access-date=2023-11-29 |website=www.iwm.org.uk}}</ref> Shortly after returning to New Jersey, they moved to Fairfax, VA, where Tom Schreiber worked as an applied mathematician and physicist at Signal Corp on Fort Monmouth. At age 61, Schreiber discovered that Tom Schreiber was not his biological father.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Schreiber |first=Stuart L. |date=July–August 2019 |title=Truth: A Love Story |work=Harvard Magazine |url=https://www.harvardmagazine.com/2019/06/dna-testing-schreiber |access-date=November 29, 2023}}</ref>

Schreiber attended Luther Jackson Junior High School in Falls Church, VA and graduated from Oakton High School in Fairfax, VA in 1973 after completing a 3-year work study program that prepared him for work in the construction field.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Werth |first=Barry |title=The Billion Dollar Molecule: One Company's quest for the perfect drug. |publisher=Simon & Schuster |year=1994 |isbn=978-0671510572 |location=United States of America |pages=197–198 |language=English}}</ref>

==Education and training==
Schreiber obtained a Bachelor of Science degree in chemistry from the [[University of Virginia]] in 1977, after which he entered Harvard University as a graduate student in chemistry. He joined the research group of [[Robert B. Woodward]] and after Woodward's death continued his studies under the supervision of [[Yoshito Kishi]]. In 1980, he joined the faculty of [[Yale University]] as an assistant professor in chemistry, and in 1988 he moved to Harvard University as the Morris Loeb Professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Department of Chemistry |url=https://chemistry.as.virginia.edu/people/profile/Stuart-Schreiber |access-date=2023-11-16 |website=chemistry.as.virginia.edu}}</ref>

==Career==
Schreiber started his research work in organic synthesis, focusing on concepts such as the use of [[Woodward-Hoffmann rules|[2 + 2] photocycloadditions]] to establish [[stereochemistry]] in complex molecules, the fragmentation of hydroperoxides to produce [[macrolides]], ancillary stereocontrol, group selectivity and two-directional synthesis. Notable accomplishments include the total syntheses of complex natural products such as periplanone B, talaromycin B, asteltoxin, avenaciolide, gloeosporone, hikizimicin, mycoticin A, epoxydictymene<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jamison|first1=Timothy F.|last2=Shambayati|first2=Soroosh|last3=Crowe|first3=William E.|last4=Schreiber|first4=Stuart L.|date=1994-06-01|title=Cobalt-Mediated Total Synthesis of (+)-Epoxydictymene|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=116|issue=12|pages=5505–5506|doi=10.1021/ja00091a079|bibcode=1994JAChS.116.5505J |issn=0002-7863}}</ref> and the immunosuppressant [[FK-506]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nakatsuka |first=Masashi |last2=Ragan |first2=John A. |last3=Sammakia |first3=Tarek |last4=Smith |first4=David B. |last5=Uehling |first5=David E. |last6=Schreiber |first6=Stuart L. |date=1990-07-01 |title=Total synthesis of FK506 and an FKBP probe reagent, [C(8),C(9)-13C2]-FK506 |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/ja00170a024 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |volume=112 |issue=14 |pages=5583–5601 |doi=10.1021/ja00170a024 |issn=0002-7863|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Following his work on the FK506-binding protein [[FKBP|FKBP12]] in 1988, Schreiber reported that the small molecules [[FK506]] and [[cyclosporin]] inhibit the activity of the phosphatase [[calcineurin]] by forming the ternary complexes FKBP12-FK506-calcineurin and cyclophilin-ciclosporin-calcineurin.<ref name=one>{{cite journal |vauthors=Liu J, Farmer JD, Lane WS, Friedman J, Weissman I, Schreiber SL |title=Calcineurin is a common target of cyclophilin-cyclosporin A and FKBP-FK506 complexes |journal=Cell |volume=66 |issue=4 |pages=807–15 |date=August 1991 |pmid=1715244 |doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90124-H|bibcode=1991Cell...66..807L |s2cid=22094672 }}</ref> This work, together with work by [[Gerald Crabtree]] at [[Stanford University]] concerning the [[NFAT]] proteins, led to the elucidation of the calcium-[[calcineurin]]-[[NFAT]] signaling pathway.<ref name=two>{{cite journal |vauthors=Schreiber SL, Crabtree GR |title=Immunophilins, ligands, and the control of signal transduction |journal=Harvey Lectures |volume=91 |pages=99–114 |year=1995 |pmid=9127988}}</ref> 

In 1993, Schreiber and Crabtree developed bifunctional molecules or “chemical inducers of proximity” (CIPs), which provide small-molecule activation over numerous signaling molecules and pathways (e.g., the Fas, insulin, [[TGFβ]] and T-cell receptors<ref name=three>{{cite journal |vauthors=Yang J, Symes K, Mercola M, Schreiber SL |title=Small-molecule control of insulin and PDGF receptor signaling and the role of membrane attachment |journal=Current Biology |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=11–8 |date=January 1998 |pmid=9427627 |doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(98)70015-6|s2cid=18682114 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1998CBio....8...11Y }}</ref><ref name=four>{{cite journal |vauthors=Stockwell BR, Schreiber SL |title=Probing the role of homomeric and heteromeric receptor interactions in TGF-beta signaling using small molecule dimerizers |journal=Current Biology |volume=8 |issue=13 |pages=761–70 |date=June 1998 |pmid=9651680 |doi=10.1016/S0960-9822(98)70299-4|s2cid=93779 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1998CBio....8..761S }}</ref>) through proximity effects. Schreiber and Crabtree demonstrated that small molecules could activate a signaling pathway in an animal with temporal and spatial control.<ref name=five>"Functional Analysis of Fas Signaling in vivo Using Synthetic Dimerizers" David Spencer, Pete Belshaw, Lei Chen, Steffan Ho, Filippo Randazzo, Gerald R. Crabtree, Stuart L. Schreiber ''Curr. Biol''. '''1996''', 6, 839–848.</ref> Dimerizer kits have been distributed freely resulting in many peer-reviewed publications.  Its promise in gene therapy has been highlighted by the ability of a small molecule to activate a small-molecule regulated EPO receptor and to induce [[erythropoiesis]] ([[ARIAD Pharmaceuticals|Ariad Pharmaceuticals]], Inc.), and more recently in human clinical trials for treatment of graft-vs-host disease.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Di Stasi|first1=Antonio|last2=Tey|first2=Siok-Keen|last3=Dotti|first3=Gianpietro|last4=Fujita|first4=Yuriko|last5=Kennedy-Nasser|first5=Alana|last6=Martinez|first6=Caridad|last7=Straathof|first7=Karin|last8=Liu|first8=Enli|last9=Durett|first9=April G.|date=2011-11-03|title=Inducible Apoptosis as a Safety Switch for Adoptive Cell Therapy|journal=New England Journal of Medicine|volume=365|issue=18|pages=1673–1683|doi=10.1056/nejmoa1106152|issn=0028-4793|pmid=22047558|pmc=3236370}}</ref>

In 1994, Schreiber and co-workers investigated (independently with [[David M. Sabatini|David Sabitini]]) the master regulator of nutrient sensing, mTOR. They found that the small molecule [[Sirolimus|rapamycin]] simultaneously binds FKBP12 and [[Mammalian target of rapamycin|mTOR]] (originally named FKBP12-rapamycin binding protein, FRAP).<ref name=six>{{cite journal  |vauthors=Brown EJ, Albers MW, Shin TB, etal |title=A mammalian protein targeted by G1-arresting rapamycin-receptor complex |journal=Nature |volume=369 |issue=6483 |pages=756–8 |date=June 1994 |pmid=8008069 |doi=10.1038/369756a0|bibcode=1994Natur.369..756B |s2cid=4359651 }}</ref> Using diversity-oriented synthesis and small-molecule screening, Schreiber illuminated the nutrient-response signaling network involving TOR proteins in yeast and mTOR in mammalian cells.  Small molecules such as uretupamine<ref name=seven>"Dissection of a glucose-sensitive pathway of the nutrient-response network using diversity-oriented synthesis and small molecule microarrays" Finny G. Kuruvilla, Alykhan F. Shamji, Scott M. Sternson, Paul J. Hergenrother, Stuart L. Schreiber, ''Nature'', '''2002''', 416, 653–656.</ref> and rapamycin were shown to be particularly effective in revealing the ability of proteins such as mTOR, Tor1p, Tor2p, and Ure2p to receive multiple inputs and to process them appropriately towards multiple outputs (in analogy to multi-channel processors).  Several pharmaceutical companies are now targeting the nutrient-signaling network for the treatment of several forms of cancer, including solid tumors.<ref name=eight>{{cite journal |vauthors=Shamji AF, Nghiem P, Schreiber SL |title=Integration of growth factor and nutrient signaling: implications for cancer biology |journal=Molecular Cell |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=271–80 |date=August 2003 |pmid=14536067 |doi=10.1016/j.molcel.2003.08.016|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 1995, Schreiber and co-workers found that the small molecule [[lactacystin]] binds and inhibits specific catalytic subunits of the [[proteasome]],<ref name="Fenteany">{{cite journal |vauthors=Fenteany G, Standaert RF, Lane WS, Choi S, Corey EJ, Schreiber SL |title=Inhibition of proteasome activities and subunit-specific amino-terminal threonine modification by lactacystin |journal=Science |volume=268 |issue=5211 |pages=726–31 |year=1995 |pmid=7732382 |doi=10.1126/science.7732382|bibcode=1995Sci...268..726F |s2cid=37779687 }}</ref> a protein complex responsible for the bulk of proteolysis in the cell, as well as proteolytic activation of certain protein substrates. As a non-peptidic proteasome inhibitor lactacysin has proven useful in the study of proteasome function. Lactacystin modifies the amino-terminal threonine of specific proteasome subunits. This work helped to establish the proteasome as a mechanistically novel class of protease: an amino-terminal [[threonine protease]]. 

In 1996, Schreiber and co-workers used the small molecules trapoxin and depudecin to investigate the [[histone deacetylase]]s (HDACs).<ref name=nine>{{cite journal |vauthors=Taunton J, Hassig CA, Schreiber SL |title=A mammalian histone deacetylase related to the yeast transcriptional regulator Rpd3p |journal=Science |volume=272 |issue=5260 |pages=408–11 |date=April 1996 |pmid=8602529 |doi=10.1126/science.272.5260.408|bibcode=1996Sci...272..408T |s2cid=25717734 }}</ref> Prior to Schreiber's work in this area, the HDAC proteins had not been isolated. Coincident with the HDAC work, [[Charles David Allis]] and colleagues reported work on the [[histone acetyltransferase]]s (HATs). These two contributions catalyzed much research in this area, eventually leading to the characterization of numerous histone-modifying enzymes, their resulting histone “marks”, and numerous proteins that bind to these marks.  By taking a global approach to understanding chromatin function, Schreiber proposed a “signaling network model” of chromatin and compared it to an alternative view, the “histone code hypothesis” presented by [[Brian D. Strahl]] and [[Charles David Allis]].<ref name=ten>{{cite journal |vauthors=Schreiber SL, Bernstein BE |title=Signaling network model of chromatin |journal=Cell |volume=111 |issue=6 |pages=771–8 |date=December 2002 |pmid=12526804 |doi=10.1016/S0092-8674(02)01196-0|s2cid=8824652 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

==Diversity-oriented synthesis==
Schreiber applied small molecules to biology through the development of diversity-oriented synthesis (DOS),<ref name=eleven>(a) {{cite journal |author=Schreiber SL |title=Target-oriented and diversity-oriented organic synthesis in drug discovery |journal=Science |volume=287 |issue=5460 |pages=1964–9 |date=March 2000 |pmid=10720315 |doi=10.1126/science.287.5460.1964|bibcode=2000Sci...287.1964S |s2cid=42413249 }} (b) {{cite journal |vauthors=Burke MD, Berger EM, Schreiber SL |title=Generating diverse skeletons of small molecules combinatorially |journal=Science |volume=302 |issue=5645 |pages=613–8 |date=October 2003 |pmid=14576427 |doi=10.1126/science.1089946|bibcode=2003Sci...302..613B |s2cid=6168881 }}  (c) {{cite journal |vauthors=Burke MD, Schreiber SL |title=A planning strategy for diversity-oriented synthesis |journal=Angewandte Chemie |volume=43 |issue=1 |pages=46–58 |date=January 2004 |pmid=14694470 |doi=10.1002/anie.200300626 |bibcode=2004ACIE...43...46B }}</ref> chemical genetics,<ref name=twelve>"The small-molecule approach to biology: Chemical genetics and diversity-oriented organic synthesis make possible the systematic exploration of biology”, S L Schreiber, ''C&E News'', '''2003''', 81, 51–61.</ref> and ChemBank.<ref name=thirteen>{{cite journal |vauthors=Strausberg RL, Schreiber SL |title=From knowing to controlling: a path from genomics to drugs using small molecule probes |journal=Science |volume=300 |issue=5617 |pages=294–5 |date=April 2003 |pmid=12690189 |doi=10.1126/science.1083395|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1230826 |bibcode=2003Sci...300..294S |s2cid=39877841 }}</ref> Schreiber has shown that DOS can produce small molecules distributed in defined ways in chemical space by virtue of their different skeletons and stereochemistry, and that it can provide chemical handles on products anticipating the need for follow-up chemistry using, for example, combinatorial synthesis and the so-called Build/Couple/Pair strategy of modular chemical synthesis. DOS pathways and new techniques for small-molecule screening<ref name=fourteen>{{cite journal |vauthors=Stockwell BR, Haggarty SJ, Schreiber SL |title=High-throughput screening of small molecules in miniaturized mammalian cell-based assays involving post-translational modifications |journal=Chemistry & Biology |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=71–83 |date=February 1999 |pmid=10021420 |doi=10.1016/S1074-5521(99)80004-0|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=fifteen>"Printing Small Molecules as Microarrays and Detecting Protein-Ligand Interactions en Masse" Gavin MacBeath, Angela N. Koehler, Stuart L. Schreiber ''J. Am. Chem. Soc.'' '''1999''', 121, 7967–7968.</ref><ref name=sixteen>{{cite journal |vauthors=MacBeath G, Schreiber SL |title=Printing proteins as microarrays for high-throughput function determination |journal=Science |volume=289 |issue=5485 |pages=1760–3 |date=September 2000 |pmid=10976071 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.289.5485.1760 |doi=10.1126/science.289.5485.1760|bibcode=2000Sci...289.1760M |s2cid=27553611 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> provided many new, potentially disruptive insights into biology.  Small-molecule probes of histone and tubulin deacetylases, transcription factors, cytoplasmic anchoring proteins, developmental signaling proteins (e.g., histacin, tubacin, haptamide, uretupamine,  concentramide, and calmodulophilin), among many others, have been uncovered in the Schreiber lab using diversity-oriented synthesis and chemical genetics. Multidimensional screening was introduced in 2002 and has provided insights into tumorigenesis, cell polarity, and chemical space, among others.<ref name=eighteen>{{cite journal |author=Schreiber SL |title=Small molecules: the missing link in the central dogma |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=64–6 |date=July 2005 |pmid=16407997 |doi=10.1038/nchembio0705-64|s2cid=14399359 }}</ref>

Using diversity-oriented synthesis, the Schreiber Lab and collaborators discovered numerous novel antimicrobial compounds including the bicyclic azetidine BRD7929 that could both cure and prevent the transmission of malaria in mice, targeting multiple steps in the life cycle of ''Plasmodium falciparum''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kato |first1=Nobutaka |last2=Comer |first2=Eamon |last3=Sakata-Kato == Other research ==
Schreiber also contributed to more conventional small molecule discovery projects. He collaborated with [[Tim Mitchison]] to discover [[monastrol]] – the first small-molecule inhibitor of [[mitosis]] that does not target [[tubulin]].<ref name="seventeen">{{cite journal |vauthors=Mayer TU, Kapoor TM, Haggarty SJ, King RW, Schreiber SL, Mitchison TJ |date=October 1999 |title=Small molecule inhibitor of mitotic spindle bipolarity identified in a phenotype-based screen |url=https://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:352-140561 |journal=Science |volume=286 |issue=5441 |pages=971–4 |doi=10.1126/science.286.5441.971 |pmid=10542155 |bibcode=1999Sci...286..971M }}</ref> [[Monastrol]] was shown to inhibit [[kinesin-5]], a motor protein and was used to gain new insights into the functions of kinesin-5. This work led pharmaceutical company Merck, among others, to pursue anti-cancer drugs that target human kinesin-5.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cox |first=Christopher D. |last2=Coleman |first2=Paul J. |last3=Breslin |first3=Michael J. |last4=Whitman |first4=David B. |last5=Garbaccio |first5=Robert M. |last6=Fraley |first6=Mark E. |last7=Buser |first7=Carolyn A. |last8=Walsh |first8=Eileen S. |last9=Hamilton |first9=Kelly |last10=Schaber |first10=Michael D. |last11=Lobell |first11=Robert B. |last12=Tao |first12=Weikang |last13=Davide |first13=Joseph P. |last14=Diehl |first14=Ronald E. |last15=Abrams |first15=Marc T. |date=2008-07-24 |title=Kinesin Spindle Protein (KSP) Inhibitors. 9. Discovery of (2S)-4-(2,5-Difluorophenyl)-N-[(3R,4S)-3-fluoro-1-methylpiperidin-4-yl]-2-(hydroxymethyl)-N-methyl-2-phenyl-2,5-dihydro-1H-pyrrole-1-carboxamide (MK-0731) for the Treatment of Taxane-Refractory Cancer |url=https://doi.org/10.1021/jm800386y |journal=Journal of Medicinal Chemistry |volume=51 |issue=14 |pages=4239–4252 |doi=10.1021/jm800386y |issn=0022-2623|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Schrieber and [[Michael T. McManus (biologist)|McManus]] discovered that when certain aggressive cancer cells become resistant to drug treatments, they also become vulnerable to ferroptosis—a natural cellular self-destruction mechanism triggered by peroxide and iron ions undergoing the Fenton reaction. Free radicals unleash a chain reaction turning normal lipids in the cell membrane into toxic radical species. They found that drug-resistant cancer cells that have acquired this new vulnerability rely on an enzyme called [[GPX4]] for survival. GPX4 stops the chain reaction leading to ferroptosis by converting the dangerous lipid peroxides to benign alcohols. They further showed that a small molecule inhibitor of GPX4 kills cancer cells by increasing their vulnerability to ferroptosis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Viswanathan |first1=Vasanthi S. |last2=Ryan |first2=Matthew J. |last3=Dhruv |first3=Harshil D. |last4=Gill |first4=Shubhroz |last5=Eichhoff |first5=Ossia M. |last6=Seashore-Ludlow |first6=Brinton |last7=Kaffenberger |first7=Samuel D. |last8=Eaton |first8=John K. |last9=Shimada |first9=Kenichi |last10=Aguirre |first10=Andrew J. |last11=Viswanathan |first11=Srinivas R. |last12=Chattopadhyay |first12=Shrikanta |last13=Tamayo |first13=Pablo |last14=Yang |first14=Wan Seok |last15=Rees |first15=Matthew G. |date=2017-07-27 |title=Dependency of a therapy-resistant state of cancer cells on a lipid peroxidase pathway |journal=Nature |volume=547 |issue=7664 |pages=453–457 |doi=10.1038/nature23007 |issn=1476-4687 |pmc=5667900 |pmid=28678785 |bibcode=2017Natur.547..453V }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Hangauer MJ, Viswanathan VS, Ryan MJ, Bole D, Eaton JK, Matov A, Galeas J, Dhruv HD, Berens ME, Schreiber SL, McCormick F, McManus MT | title = Drug-tolerant persister cancer cells are vulnerable to GPX4 inhibition | journal = Nature | volume = 551 | issue = 7679 | pages = 247–250 | date = November 2017 | pmid = 29088702 | pmc = 5933935 | doi = 10.1038/nature24297 | bibcode = 2017Natur.551..247H }}</ref>

== Impact on chemical biology ==
Schreiber has used small molecules to study three specific areas of biology, and then through the more general application of small molecules in biomedical research. Academic screening centers have been created that emulate the Harvard Institute of Chemistry and Cell Biology and the Broad Institute; in the U.S., there has been a nationwide effort to expand this capability via the government-sponsored NIH Road Map. Chemistry departments have changed their names to include the term chemical biology and new journals have been introduced (Cell Chemical Biology, ChemBioChem, Nature Chemical Biology, ACS Chemical Biology]) to cover the field.  Schreiber has been involved in the founding of numerous biopharmaceutical companies whose research relies on chemical biology: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (VRTX), Ariad Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (ARIA), Infinity Pharmaceuticals, Inc (INFI), Forma Therapeutics, H3 Biomedicine, Jnana Therapeutics, and Kojin Therapeutics.  These companies have produced new therapeutics in several disease areas, including [[cystic fibrosis]] and cancer.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wainwright |first1=Claire E. |last2=Elborn |first2=J. Stuart |last3=Ramsey |first3=Bonnie W. |last4=Marigowda |first4=Gautham |last5=Huang |first5=Xiaohong |last6=Cipolli |first6=Marco |last7=Colombo |first7=Carla |last8=Davies |first8=Jane C. |last9=De Boeck |first9=Kris |date=2015-07-16 |title=Lumacaftor–Ivacaftor in Patients with Cystic Fibrosis Homozygous for Phe508del CFTR |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |volume=373 |issue=3 |pages=220–231 |doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1409547 |issn=0028-4793 |pmc=4764353 |pmid=25981758}}</ref>
